title: History & Landscape
blurb: Tests the three eras of AI, the nesting of AI, ML and deep learning, the roles around a project, when classical ML beats deep learning, and the first pandas procedures the rest of the book relies on.

ideas.title: The three eras and what limited each
AI, machine learning and deep learning as nested subsets
Roles, the AI stack and the Solutions Architect's job
Deep learning vs classical ML vs foundation models
First inspection, selecting, filtering and grouping
Derived columns, growth rates and answering a question from data

questions.prompt: The chapter says the Rules & Expert Systems era did not end for lack of compute or algorithms. What was the bottleneck that ended it?
options: Labelled data. There were not yet large labelled datasets to test the rules against.
Compute. Rule engines needed far more processing power than 1970s and 1980s hardware gave.
Interpretability. Regulators could not follow the long chains of if/then rules.
Knowledge acquisition. Hand-coding what experts know took longer than training the experts.
questions.explanation: The chapter names knowledge acquisition as the bottleneck. Complex domains cannot be hand-coded, so they have to be learned from data. Compute and data were the limits of the *next* era (Statistical ML), where neural networks existed but took too long to train. Rule systems are, if anything, easy to interpret.

questions.prompt: Which statement matches the nesting of terms in this chapter?
options: Deep learning is a subset of machine learning, which is a subset of AI.
Machine learning and deep learning are separate branches of AI with no overlap.
AI is a subset of machine learning, which is a subset of deep learning.
Machine learning is a subset of deep learning, which is a subset of AI.
questions.explanation: AI is the broadest term. Machine learning is the part of AI that learns from data. Deep learning is the part of machine learning that uses neural networks. So every deep learning system is ML and AI, but a hand-coded expert system is AI without being ML. The 'separate branches' option is the common mistake of thinking deep learning is not machine learning.

questions.prompt: Foundation models are becoming a commodity. According to the chapter, where does an enterprise AI system's differentiation now come from?
options: Data quality, fine-tuning, and the operational layer around the model.
Picking whichever foundation model has the largest parameter count available.
Writing a custom neural network architecture for each use case.
Replacing the data engineering layer with a foundation model.
questions.explanation: The chapter says the differentiation is in data quality, fine-tuning, and the operational layer, which is most of the book. If every customer can call the same large model, model size alone gives no edge. Data engineering sits *below* the foundation model layer in the stack. It is not replaced by it.

questions.prompt: Select ALL situations where the chapter says classical ML still wins over deep learning.
options: Raw images where the useful features are not known in advance.
A regulated setting where each decision must be explained.
Tens of millions of unlabelled audio clips.
Tabular data with clear features, as in most enterprise datasets.
A few thousand labelled examples rather than millions.
questions.explanation: Classical ML wins on tabular data with clear features, in low-data regimes, where interpretability is required, and on speed and cost. Deep learning is better on unstructured data (images, audio, text, video), on tasks where the features are not known in advance, and when training data is massive.

questions.prompt: You load a new CSV. Which single command from Procedure 1.1 tells you both that a date column came in as `object` and how many non-null values each column has?
options: `df.info()`
`df.describe()`
`df.shape`
`df.head()`
questions.explanation: `df.info()` lists column names, dtypes and non-null counts. `df.describe()` gives summary statistics, by default only for numeric columns, so it would skip an `object` date column rather than flag it. `df.head()` shows the first 5 rows and `df.shape` only gives (rows, columns).

questions.prompt: `df['yoy_change'] = df['value'].pct_change() * 100` puts `NaN` in the first row. What is the right reading of that?
options: A bug. `pct_change()` needs the column sorted descending first.
Expected. The first row has no prior value to compare against.
A bug. The first value in the column must be missing.
Expected. `pct_change()` always skips the row with the largest value.
questions.explanation: Percentage change needs a previous value, and the first row has none. The chapter calls this expected, not a bug. Drop it with `.dropna()` or fill it with `.fillna(0)` depending on what the chart needs. It does not mean the underlying value is missing.

questions.prompt: A team spends most of its effort cleaning, deduplicating and curating a very large text corpus. They hand-craft no features. The network learns its own internal representations straight from tokens. Which era's pattern of human effort is this?
options: Statistical Machine Learning, 1980s to 2010s
Rules & Expert Systems, 1950s to 1980s
Deep Learning & Foundation Models, 2012 on
questions.explanation: In Era 3 the model learns representations end-to-end from raw pixels or tokens. What is left for the human is preparing and curating data at scale, which the chapter calls feature engineering pushed up to the level of the whole dataset. Era 2 is the tempting wrong answer, but there the human effort went into crafting individual features by hand. In Era 1 it went into writing rules.

questions.prompt: Select ALL systems that count as **machine learning** under the chapter's definitions.
options: A convolutional neural network trained to classify X-rays.
A logistic regression fitted to labelled churn data.
An expert system whose rules were typed in by doctors.
A Random Forest trained on past loan outcomes.
A hand-coded if/then system that flags any transaction over 10,000 dollars.
questions.explanation: Machine learning means learning from data rather than being explicitly programmed. The Random Forest and the logistic regression are classical ML. The CNN is deep learning, which is a subset of ML, so it counts too. The two hand-coded rule systems are AI (or plain software) but not ML, because nobody learned the rules from data.

questions.prompt: A customer's churn model scores well in the notebook. Once deployed, nobody notices when latency spikes or input data shifts, and there is no monitoring. Which role's core focus covers this gap?
options: Data Scientist
ML Engineer
Data Engineer
Data Analyst
questions.explanation: The ML Engineer makes models work reliably in production: MLOps, serving and monitoring. The Data Scientist built the model and is the tempting answer, but their focus is building models that predict or explain. The Data Engineer builds the pipelines that move and store data. The Data Analyst describes what the data says now.

questions.prompt: A bank has 40,000 rows of tabular loan data with clear features. A regulator requires an explanation for each declined application. Which approach does the chapter point to?
options: An LLM-orchestrated multi-agent pipeline that writes each decision.
Logistic regression with SHAP explanations.
Train a CNN on images of the loan application forms.
Fine-tune a large foundation model on the loan rows.
questions.explanation: Tabular data, clear features, a modest row count and a hard interpretability need all point to classical ML. The Quick Reference maps 'tabular data, need to explain decisions' to logistic regression plus SHAP. A foundation model would cost more, be harder to explain, and is unlikely to be more accurate on this data.

questions.prompt:
What value does this code print for category `A`? Give a number to 1 decimal place.

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

df = pd.DataFrame({
    'category': ['A', 'A', 'A', 'B'],
    'value':    [10, 20, np.nan, 5],
})
print(df.groupby('category')['value'].mean())
```
questions.explanation: `mean()` skips `NaN` by default. Group A has the non-missing values 10 and 20, so the mean is $(10+20)/2 = 15.0$. The tempting wrong answer is $30/3 = 10.0$, which treats the missing value as a zero. That is also why Procedure 1.1 asks you to check `df.isnull().sum()` before trusting grouped summaries.

questions.prompt: A yearly paper count is `[4, 5, 8, 6]`. After `yoy = s.pct_change() * 100`, what is the largest value in `yoy`? Give a percentage to 1 decimal place.
questions.explanation: `pct_change()` gives $(x_t - x_{t-1})/x_{t-1}$. The values are NaN, $(5-4)/4 = 25\%$, $(8-5)/5 = 60\%$ and $(6-8)/8 = -25\%$. The largest is 60.0%. A common slip is to divide by the new value, giving $3/8 = 37.5\%$.

questions.prompt:
What year does this code print? Give an integer.

```python
df = pd.DataFrame({
    'year':          [2008, 2009, 2010, 2011, 2012],
    'classical_ml':  [5, 6, 7, 8, 9],
    'deep_learning': [2, 4, 7, 9, 15],
})
df['dl_vs_classical'] = df['deep_learning'] - df['classical_ml']
crossover = df[df['dl_vs_classical'] > 0].iloc[0]
print(int(crossover['year']))
```
questions.explanation: The differences are $-3, -2, 0, 1, 6$. The filter is strictly `> 0`, so 2010, where the two are tied at 7, is excluded. The first row that passes is 2011. Answering 2010 confuses 'caught up with' and 'exceeded'.

questions.prompt: In the late 1980s ALVINN replaced hand-written steering rules with a neural network trained by backpropagation. A colleague says this proves it belongs to the Deep Learning era. What is the best response using the chapter's account?
options: Deep Learning. Any system that uses a neural network belongs to Era 3 by definition, whatever its date.
Rules & Expert Systems, because it was built before 2012 and before GPUs existed.
Statistical ML. Neural nets and backprop existed, but data and compute limited what they could learn.
Deep Learning, because Era 3 began when backpropagation was rediscovered in 1986 by Rumelhart et al.
questions.explanation: Eras are defined by what drove the field and what limited it, not by whether a neural network appears. Backpropagation was rediscovered in 1986 and sits in Era 2. The chapter says the limit of that era was data and compute: neural networks existed, but training them on anything interesting took too long. Era 3 starts in 2012, when large labelled datasets and GPUs arrived. ALVINN learns from data, so it is not a rules system either.

questions.prompt: A vendor pitches: "Our fraud product uses AI, not just machine learning, so it is more advanced." Using the nesting relation, what is the best analysis?
options: The claim holds. AI sits inside deep learning, which is the newest and most advanced subset of all.
The claim is empty, but only because AI and machine learning are two names for the same thing.
The claim holds. AI is the superset, so it must include deep learning and go beyond plain ML.
'AI but not ML' implies hand-coded rules. Being in the broader set says nothing about being advanced.
questions.explanation: Because ML is a subset of AI, 'AI but not ML' can only describe the part of AI that does not learn from data, such as a hand-coded rules engine. That is the approach the field moved away from. Being in a superset does not mean including every member of it. The 'synonyms' option reaches a similar verdict for the wrong reason. The chapter's point is that the terms are not synonyms.

questions.prompt: A data scientist has turned the ask into a measurable target. The product manager says the budget covers a 3-month build. The ML engineer says real-time serving needs 6 months. The two sides disagree about feasibility. By the chapter's account, who owns this conversation and what is the move?
options: The ML engineer, who should decide alone because serving and latency are their area.
A research scientist, who should be brought in to design a faster real-time serving architecture.
The Solutions Architect. Translate both ways, e.g. propose nightly batch scoring that fits the budget.
The data scientist, who should renegotiate the business goal because they defined the modelling problem.
questions.explanation: The chapter says the Solutions Architect translates between the technical roles and the business side and owns the feasibility conversation when they disagree. A data scientist's responsibility usually stops at turning the ask into a measurable modelling problem, which is why that option is tempting but wrong. The ML engineer has one side of the trade-off, not the business side. Research scientists advance the state of the art and do not own customer trade-offs.

questions.prompt: A team trains a large transformer from scratch on 800 labelled rows of tabular data. Training loss jumps around between runs and the result is worse than a logistic regression. Which limit from §1.3 best explains this?
options: Classical ML's limit. The features were hand-crafted, so no model of any kind can do better than those features.
Tabular data is unstructured, so the transformer needed more layers and more epochs than the team used.
Foundation models' limit. A general model needs fine-tuning or retrieval before it does one specific task well.
Deep learning's limit. Too little data and compute, so a large net won't beat a simple model or train stably.
questions.explanation: The chapter says deep learning's ceiling is compute and data. Without enough of both, a large network will not beat a simpler model and often will not train stably. Both symptoms appear here. The foundation-model option is tempting, but this model was trained from scratch, not adapted from a pretrained one. Tabular data is structured, which is why classical ML suits it.

questions.prompt:
A colleague writes this filter and it fails. What is the cause?

```python
recent_dl = df[df['year'] > 2010 & df['subfield'] == 'deep_learning']
```
options: `&` binds tighter than `>` and `==`, so `2010 & df['subfield']` runs first. Each condition needs parentheses.
`df['year'] > 2010` returns a plain Python list rather than a Series, so it cannot be used to index `df`.
`&` does not work on pandas Series. The element-wise AND should be written with the keyword `and`.
Comparing strings inside a boolean filter needs `.str.contains()`, because `==` is not supported for text.
questions.explanation: In Python, `&` has higher precedence than comparisons. The expression becomes `df['year'] > (2010 & df['subfield']) == 'deep_learning'`, and `2010 & <string Series>` raises a `TypeError`. The fix in Listing 1.2 is `(df['year'] > 2010) & (df['subfield'] == 'deep_learning')`. Switching to `and` is the tempting wrong fix: it raises `ValueError: The truth value of a Series is ambiguous`.

questions.prompt: Yearly paper counts for a new subfield, 2001 to 2005, are `[0, 0, 2, 4, 5]`. You compute `growth = s.pct_change() * 100` and want the single largest *legitimate* growth year. What growth value should you report? Give a percentage to 1 decimal place.
questions.explanation: The growth values are NaN (no prior year), NaN for 2002 ($0/0$), `inf` for 2003 ($2/0$), 100% for 2004 ($(4-2)/2$) and 25% for 2005. `growth.nlargest(1)` would rank the `inf` first. That is the artifact the chapter warns about, not a real growth rate. Excluding it (for example with `growth.replace([np.inf, -np.inf], np.nan).dropna()`) leaves 100.0% in 2004. Like the book's 1998 result, it is still a low-base effect on tiny counts.

questions.prompt: A customer has 5,000 rows of tabular account data and wants a weekly churn score. Their team proposes an LLM-orchestrated multi-agent system that reads each account and writes a risk score. Select ALL critiques that the chapter supports.
options: Classical models cannot be explained, so the LLM is the only option if the regulator asks why.
A general foundation model needs adaptation before it does one enterprise task well, and that step has its own cost.
A weekly batch score can come from a static, deterministic pipeline. Orchestration adds cost without a clear need.
Deep learning cannot process tabular data at all, so the proposal cannot run.
Tabular data with clear features and a few thousand rows is where gradient-boosted trees usually win on accuracy and cost.
questions.explanation: The first three follow from §1.3. Classical ML wins on tabular, low-data problems. The chapter names 'a multi-agent, LLM-orchestrated mess when a static, deterministic pipeline is all that's needed' as a common mistake. Foundation models' limit is their generality. The last two are wrong. Deep learning *can* run on tabular data, it is not the best tool here. Interpretability is a strength of classical ML, not a weakness.

questions.prompt:
The rows below arrived in the order the source system exported them. What year does the code print? Give an integer.

```python
df = pd.DataFrame({
    'year':          [2014, 2011, 2012, 2013, 2010],
    'classical_ml':  [9.0, 7.0, 7.5, 8.0, 6.0],
    'deep_learning': [30.0, 8.0, 11.0, 18.0, 5.0],
})
df['dl_vs_classical'] = df['deep_learning'] - df['classical_ml']
crossover = df[df['dl_vs_classical'] > 0].iloc[0]
print(int(crossover['year']))
```
questions.explanation: The differences in row order are $21, 1, 3.5, 10, -1$. `.iloc[0]` takes the first row *by position* among those that pass the filter, which is the 2014 row. The true first crossover year is 2011, but Listing 1.7 only finds it when the data is sorted by year. Add `df = df.sort_values('year')` first. Answering 2011 means you assumed the order. This is why the first inspection with `df.head()` matters.

questions.prompt:
Paper counts for 2020 are missing in the source. What does the last line show, and why?

```python
df = pd.DataFrame({
    'year':   [2019, 2019, 2020, 2020, 2021, 2021],
    'papers': [3, 1, np.nan, np.nan, 6, 2],
})
yearly = df.groupby('year')['papers'].sum()
growth = yearly.pct_change() * 100
print(growth.nlargest(1))
```
options: An error. `groupby().sum()` refuses to aggregate a group with only missing values.
2021 with 100.0. `pct_change()` skips the missing 2020 and compares 8 with 4.
2021 with `inf`. `sum()` turns the all-NaN 2020 group into 0, so growth is $8/0$.
2021 with `NaN`. The missing 2020 values propagate through `sum()` and `pct_change()`.
questions.explanation: `sum()` skips NaN, and the sum of an empty set is 0. So 2020 becomes 0, not NaN. Growth for 2020 is $-100\%$ and for 2021 it is $(8-0)/0$, which is `inf`. `nlargest` ranks that value first. Missing data (Procedure 1.1) has turned into the zero-to-nonzero artifact from §1.5. The fix is to handle missing years before aggregating, for example with `sum(min_count=1)` so the group stays NaN.

questions.prompt: In a dataset, classical ML papers grow from 4.0k in 2012 to 9.0k in 2024, while deep learning grows from 8.0k to 450k. A stakeholder concludes "classical ML research is dying". Which reading of the numbers is correct?
options: Right. A 50 to 1 ratio in 2024 means classical ML output shrank by a factor of about 50 since 2010.
Wrong. Classical ML more than doubled. Deep learning grew far faster, so the ratio rose to about 50 to 1.
Wrong. The ratio stayed at about 2 to 1 over the whole period, since both fields grew every year.
Right. Classical ML's share of all papers fell, which means its yearly paper count fell in absolute terms.
questions.explanation: Classical ML went from 4.0k to 9.0k, a factor of $9.0/4.0 = 2.25$, so it grew. The ratio went from $8.0/4.0 = 2$ to $450/9.0 = 50$. The chapter's own reading is that classical ML kept growing at a roughly constant rate while deep learning grew exponentially around it. A falling share does not mean a falling count, which is the mistake in the second option.

bookExercises.prompt: Name the era (Rules & Expert Systems / Statistical ML / Deep Learning & Foundation Models) each of the following belongs to, and give one reason it belongs there: (a) Random Forests; (b) BERT; (c) MYCIN.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: (a) Random Forests: Statistical ML; an ensemble of decision trees learned from labelled examples, no hand-coded rules. (b) BERT: Deep Learning & Foundation Models; a pretrained transformer, part of the post-2012 scale-driven era. (c) MYCIN: Rules & Expert Systems; a hand-coded if-then medical diagnosis system from the 1970s, predating any learning from data.

bookExercises.prompt: Explain in one or two sentences why "AI," "machine learning," and "deep learning" are not synonyms, using the nesting relationship from this chapter.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: They're nested subsets, not synonyms. Artificial Intelligence is the broadest term: any system exhibiting intelligent behaviour, including hand-coded rule systems. Machine Learning is the subset of AI that learns from data rather than being explicitly programmed. Deep Learning is the subset of ML that specifically uses neural networks. Every deep learning system is machine learning and AI. But not every AI system is machine learning (expert systems aren't), and not every ML system is deep learning (Random Forests aren't).

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 1.6 as a starting point, add three milestones of your choosing from outside this chapter's list (they can be from any era). Then, using Procedure 1.2, determine how many of the resulting milestones fall after the year 2017.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The answer depends on the three milestones chosen. The mechanical step: append the new rows, then run `df_milestones[df_milestones['year'] > 2017]` (Procedure 1.2) and count the resulting rows. Any milestone dated 2018 or later (BERT, GPT-3, ChatGPT, GPT-4, etc.) will count; anything from Era 1 or Era 2 will not.

bookExercises.prompt: Reproduce Listing 1.7's logic to find the year deep learning paper volume first exceeded reinforcement learning paper volume in the arXiv dataset. Report the ratio between them by 2024.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: On the curated dataset, deep learning paper volume first exceeds reinforcement learning volume in **2010** as well (deep learning 12.0k vs. reinforcement learning 9.0k that year). That's the same year as the classical-ML crossover, reflecting how sharply the whole deep learning-adjacent cluster accelerated together. By 2024, deep learning outnumbers reinforcement learning by roughly **1.35x** (650k vs. 480k). That's a far smaller gap than the 50x seen against classical ML. Reinforcement learning research also grew quickly across the same period, rather than being dwarfed by it.

bookExercises.prompt: A customer's data science team has 3,000 labelled examples of a tabular fraud-detection problem and is proposing to fine-tune a foundation model for it. Using this chapter's Trade-offs section, write the two or three sentences you'd say to them. Include what you'd suggest they try first.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Something like: "With 3,000 labelled examples on a tabular problem, a foundation model is very unlikely to beat a well-tuned XGBoost or LightGBM model on accuracy. It will also cost more to run and be harder to explain to a regulator or auditor. I'd suggest starting with gradient-boosted trees as a baseline this week. If that doesn't hit the target, we can talk about where a foundation model might help. But it's not the first thing to reach for here." The point is to redirect from "AI" as a default answer. The answer should be a specific technique matched to data volume, data type, and interpretability needs.

bookExercises.prompt: The chapter notes that `pct_change()` on a zero-to-nonzero transition produces an infinite percentage. Propose two different ways to handle this before ranking growth years with `nlargest()`. State a situation where each would be the wrong choice.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Two options. (1) Explicitly filter or mask the first nonzero transition (or any `inf`/`NaN` value) before calling `nlargest()`, e.g. `growth.replace([np.inf, -np.inf], np.nan).dropna()`. This is the wrong choice if a genuine, very large but finite growth spike should be preserved: a blanket `inf` filter can be too aggressive if applied without checking what's being excluded. (2) Add a minimum-volume floor (e.g. only consider percentage growth once the series exceeds some absolute threshold, like 1k papers/year), so early near-zero noise never enters the ranking at all. This is the wrong choice if the point of the analysis is specifically to capture *early* inflection points before volume is large. That's exactly what this filter would discard.

bookExercises.prompt: Read the Domingos essay cited above. Pick one "useful thing" from it that this chapter did not mention. Explain how it would have changed the way Listing 1.7's finding was interpreted if applied to it.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Discussion only. No single answer. Domingos' essay makes the point (among others) that "more data beats a cleverer algorithm" up to a point, and that feature engineering matters more than the choice of learning algorithm for most practical problems. Applied to Listing 1.7's finding: the 2010 crossover and the subsequent 50x gap by 2024 could be read as "deep learning is a better algorithm." Domingos' framing suggests a different reading. Deep learning unlocked the ability to *use* far more data, with far less hand-engineered feature work than classical ML. That's consistent with this chapter's account of GPU compute and large labelled datasets as the real enablers, not a sudden algorithmic insight in isolation.
